blocks.html: Real robots run many programs at once: one reads the lidar, one plans a path, one drives the motors. ROS 2 (Robot Operating System 2) is a free set of tools that lets them talk. It is not an operating system; it runs on top of one.

Each program is a node that does one job. Nodes send messages on named topics. A publisher sends; any number of subscribers receive. Neither needs to know about the other, only the topic's name and message type.

blocks.name: rb-ros
blocks.cap: Nodes passing messages on topics. Stop the camera node and see who notices.

blocks.html: Splitting a robot into small nodes means each can be written, tested and restarted alone. Swap a real camera for a simulated one, and the rest of the robot never knows. That is why most research and many companies build on ROS 2.

blocks.title: Message count
blocks.q: A lidar node publishes at 10 Hz. How many scans in a minute?

blocks.html: Building one giant program, or forgetting that a topic with no publisher stays silent. A node waiting for a topic that nobody publishes just waits.

Getting set up
  • ROS 2 runs best on Ubuntu Linux. Each ROS 2 release is tied to an Ubuntu version; the official documentation lists which goes with which.
  • \$0: install it on a spare computer or in a virtual machine, and use the built-in turtlesim and the Gazebo simulator; no robot needed.
  • About \$100 to \$200 more: a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 on your mobile robot, talking to your laptop over Wi-Fi.

Work through the official beginner tutorials in order: install, turtlesim, nodes, topics. Run ros2 topic list and ros2 topic echo to watch messages go by. Then write a tiny publisher and subscriber of your own in Python.

blocks.html: Topics stream data. Sometimes a node needs to ask a question, or start a long job.
A service is one request and one reply, like asking a question. An action is for long jobs: you send a goal, get steady feedback, receive a result, and can cancel along the way.

blocks.html: Picking the right tool keeps the robot responsive. A service call to a two-minute job would leave the caller with no news and no way to stop it.

blocks.html: When many people write nodes for one robot, they must agree on units and directions. ROS has written agreements called REPs; REP 103 sets units and axes.

REP 103: use SI units: meters, seconds, kilograms, radians (and m/s, rad/s). Frames are right-handed. On a robot's body: $x$ forward, $y$ left, $z$ up. Positive rotation about $z$ is counterclockwise seen from above, so a positive turn is to the left.

blocks.name: rb-frames
blocks.cap: The robot's body frame: $x$ forward, $y$ to its left.

blocks.html: A node that publishes centimeters or degrees, while every other node expects meters and radians, gives answers off by a factor of 100 or 57. Agreeing once, in writing, avoids a whole family of bugs.

blocks.title: Convert
blocks.q: A heading of 45° in a ROS 2 message?

blocks.html: Publishing degrees or centimeters where every other node expects radians and meters.

blocks.html: A camera on the robot's head sees a ball. Where is the ball on the map? It takes a chain of frames to answer.

Each transform says how one frame sits in another: a rotation and a shift. To move a point from the camera frame to the map, apply camera → base, then base → map, working outward. In ROS 2 the tf2 library keeps this chain up to date over time.

blocks.name: rb-frames
blocks.cap: A point seen in the robot's frame, placed on the map by rotate-then-shift.

blocks.html: The order matters because rotating and shifting do not commute: rotate then shift is a different move from shift then rotate. Working outward from the frame where the point was measured always gives the right order.

blocks.title: Base to map
blocks.q: Robot at (2, 3), heading 90°. Point $(1, 0)$ in the base frame.

blocks.html: Applying the transforms in the wrong order.

blocks.html: Simulators let you test a robot that you have not built, or test a risky move without breaking anything. Gazebo is the simulator most often used with ROS 2.

A simulator advances the world in fixed time steps $\Delta t$: compute forces, update speeds, update positions, repeat. The real-time factor is simulated time divided by clock time: below 1 it runs slower than life, above 1 faster.

blocks.name: rb-pid
blocks.cap: This picture is a tiny simulation itself: it steps a cart's motion forward in small time steps.

blocks.html: Smaller steps follow the true motion more closely but take more work; too large a step can make a simulation blow up. A slow real-time factor does not make the physics wrong, it only takes longer to watch. The catch with all simulation: real motors, friction and sensors differ from the model, so a design must still be tested on hardware.
Thinking a slow simulation gives wrong answers, or that a large time step is always fine.

Spawn a simple wheeled robot in Gazebo following the ROS 2 and Gazebo tutorials, drive it from the keyboard, and record its odometry topic. Then run your encoder-square test from the Navigation course in simulation and compare the drift with your real robot's.
